rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣalawāt is an Arabized form of Syriac ṣlotha, meaning a place of prayer in Hebrew; the ordinary form is apparently a generic noun, not a proper name.
rows.anchor: معرب صلوثا بالثاء المثلثة والقصر ومعناها بالعبرانية المصلى

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء والجحدري وأبو العالية ومجاهد
rows.claim: They read ṣalawāt in the Syriac-like form ṣlotha, with thāʾ and a shortened ending.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي رجاء والجحدري وأبي العالية ومجاهد أنهم قرأوا بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hārūn's report from Abū ʿAmr of an uninflected, diptote form suggests a generic proper name; a specific place-name is unlikely, and the usual-reading explanation by resemblance to a plural is strained.
rows.anchor: ما رواه هارون عن أبي عمرو من عدم تنوينه ومنع صرفه للعلمية والعجمية

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar read the word with ḍamma on both ṣād and lām; Ibn Khalawayh also reports a kasra on ṣād with a still lām, attributed as well to al-Jahdari.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر بن محمد رضي الله تعالى عنهما ( صلوات ) بضم الصاد واللام وحكى عنه ابن خالويه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh reports a form with ḍamma on ṣād and fatḥa on lām, attributed to al-Kalbi.
rows.anchor: وحكى عنه أيضا ( صلوات ) بضم الصاد وفتح اللام وحكيت عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: In one transmission, Abū al-ʿĀliya read the word with fatḥa on ṣād and sukūn on lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو العالية في رواية ( صلوات ) بفتح الصاد وسكون اللام

rows.speaker: الحجاج بن يوسف والجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥajjāj read with ḍamma on both consonants and no alif; the same reading is also attributed to al-Jahdari.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحجاج بن يوسف ( صلوات ) بضم الصاد واللام من غير ألف وحكيت عن الجحدري

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid read ṣalūta, with two ḍammas, a tāʾ, and a following alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد ( صلوتا ) بضمتين وتاء مثناة بعدها ألف

rows.speaker: الضحاك والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbi read ṣalūth with two ḍammas, no alif, and the three-dotted thāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك والكلبي ( صلوث ) بضمتين من غير ألف وبثاء مثلثة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima read ṣalwīthā with kasra on ṣād, a still lām, kasra on wāw, then yāʾ, thāʾ, and alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة ( صلويثا ) بكسر الصاد وإسكان اللام وواو مكسورة

rows.speaker: الجحدري ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari read ṣalwāth with ḍamma on ṣād and fatḥa on wāw; Mujāhid is also reported with that form but a kasra on ṣād.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن الجحدري أيضا ( صلواث ) بضم الصاد وسكون اللام وواو مفتوحة

rows.speaker: الحجاج والجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥajjāj and al-Jahdari are reported to read ṣulūb, treating it as the irregular plural of ṣalīb on the fuʿūl pattern.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن خالوية وابن عطية عن الحجاج والجحدري ( صلوب ) بضمتين وباء موحدة على أنه جمع صليب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word has an unusually large number of variant readings.
rows.anchor: فهذه عدة قراآت قلما يوجد مثلها في كلمة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masājid are the familiar Muslim places of worship; the name honors them because prostration brings a servant closest to God.
rows.anchor: وهو معبد معروف للمسلمين وخص بهذا الاسم اعتناء بشأنه من حيث أن السجود أقرب ما يكون العبد فيه إلى ربه عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the name is exclusive because prostration in prayer belongs only to Muslims is refuted by Mary being commanded to prostrate; taking her prostration only lexically is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: لاختصاص السجود في الصلاة بالمسليمن ورد بقوله تعالى ( يا مريم اقنتي لربك واسجدي واركعي ) مع الراكعين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the named worship places occur across communities, except that biʿa is specifically Christian in the customary usage of each language.
rows.anchor: الأسماء المذكورة تشترك الأمم في مسمياتها لا البيعة فإنها مختصة بالنصارى في عرف كل لغة

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most commentators identify monasteries with monks, churches with Christians, synagogues with Jews, and mosques with Muslims.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على أن الصوامع للرهبان والبيع للنصارى والصلوات لليهود والمساجد للمسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delayed mention of mosques may follow the historical order of the institutions, place them beside praise of their worshippers, or distance them from the mention of demolition; ṣalawāt may be delayed to pair it with mosques.
rows.anchor: ولعل تأخير ذكرها مع أن الظاهر تقديمها لشرفها لأن الترتيب الوجودي كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed ordering rises in dignity: churches exceed monk-only cells in worshippers, Jewish synagogues are older, and mosques are highest because they host forms of worship absent elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنما جيء المتعبدات على هذا النسق للانتقال من شريف إلى أشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened demolition is hyperbole for widespread corruption and disruption among people if God did not empower the righteous against the wicked, rather than merely destruction of religious buildings.
rows.anchor: المبالغة في ظهور الفساد ووقوع الاختلال في أمر العباد لو لا تسليط الله تعالى المحقين على المبطلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about frequent remembrance is an adjective specifically describing mosques.
rows.anchor: في موضع الصفة لمساجد وقال الضحاك ومقاتل والكلبي

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, and al-Kalbi take the remembrance clause as describing all the worship places; Abū Ḥayyān favors this scope.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك ومقاتل والكلبي : في موضع الصفة للجميع واستظهره أبو حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abrogation of earlier laws does not preclude God's name continuing to be remembered in those places; the verse also applies generally to the period before abrogation.
rows.anchor: لأن الانتساخ لا ينافي بقاءها ببركة ذكر الله تعالى فيها مع أن معنى الآية عام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises help to whoever supports His religion or His allies, and fulfilled this by giving the Emigrants and Helpers victory over Arab, Persian, and Roman powers and their lands.
rows.anchor: وبالله لينصرن الله تعالى من ينصر دينه أو من ينصر أولياءه ولقد أنجز الله تعالى وعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is powerful to accomplish His purposes, including granting them victory.
rows.anchor: على ما يريده من مراداته التي من جملتها نصرهم ( عزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is mighty: nothing can resist or oppose Him.
rows.anchor: لا يمانعه شيء ولا يدافعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mansak means a distinct religious law assigned to each community; fronting “for every community” restricts each one to its own prescribed law.
rows.anchor: جعلنا ( وضعنا وعينا ( منسكا ( أي شريعة خاصة وتقديم الجار والمجرور على الفعل للقصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is like assigning each of four named women a different garment: no community shares or independently crosses into another's assigned law.
rows.anchor: وحاصل المعنى هنا عينا كل شريعة لأمة معينة من الأمم بحيث لا تتخطى أمة منهم شريعتها المعينة لها إلى شريعة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is an adjective reinforcing the restriction: each specifically designated community practices its own law, not another's.
rows.anchor: صفة لمنسكا مؤكدة للقصر والضمير لكل أمة باعتبار خصوصها أي تلك الأمة المعينة ناسكون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community from Moses to Jesus followed the Torah, the community from Jesus to Muhammad the Gospel, and the community beginning with Muhammad follows only the Qurʾān until the end of time.
rows.anchor: الأمة التي كانت من مبعث موسى إلى مبعث عيسى عليهما السلام منسكهم ما في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion is that the People of Scripture must not dispute the Prophet's religion by claiming their ancestors' Torah or Gospel remains binding after its abrogation.
rows.anchor: موجب لطاعة هؤلاء له صلى الله عليه وسلم وعدم منازعتهم إياه في أمر الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading is a real prohibition directed at them; the alternative makes it an indirect instruction for the Prophet to ignore their dispute, which better suits the next command but departs from the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن المراد نهيهم حقيقة عن النزاع في ذلك

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes the prohibition as a metonymic command to the Prophet not to dispute with them, as in “do not let Zayd fight you,” though the author questions the analogy for reciprocal verbs.
rows.anchor: هو نهي له عليه الصلاة والسلام على منازعتهم كما تقول : لا يضاربنك زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads the verb with a light nūn.
rows.anchor: فلا ينازعنك ) بالنون الخفيفة وقرأ أبو مجلز

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز ولاحق بن حميد
rows.claim: Abū Majliz and Lāḥiq ibn Ḥumayd read “fa-lā yanziʿannaka,” with kasra on zāy, from the verb meaning to pull or draw away.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو مجلز ولاحق بن حميد ( فلا ينزعنك ) بكسر الزاي على أنه من النزع

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī explains the variant as “do not let them pull you from your religion to theirs,” so you seem uprooted from one position to another.
rows.anchor: كما قال ابن جني فلا يستخفنك عن دينك إلى أديانهم فتكون بصورة المنزوع عن شيء إلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that this intensifies the Prophet's firmness by stirring his zeal and anger for God and His religion, a device common in the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: التثبيت له عليه الصلاة والسلام بما يهيج حميته ويلهب غضبه لله تعالى ولدينه ومثله كثير في القرآن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the command urges the Prophet to stand firm so they cannot pull him away, stirring his zeal and anger for God and His religion.
rows.anchor: التثبيت له عليه الصلاة والسلام بما يهيج حميته ويلهب غضبه لله تعالى ولدينه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives the expression from mutual disputation followed by one party prevailing: “do not let them defeat you in argument.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : هو من نازعته فنزعته أنزعه أي غلبته فالمعنى لا يغلبنك في المنازعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For most grammarians, the prevailing form in this verb class takes ḍamma on the second radical; the claimed guttural exception is rejected by scholars, making al-Zajjāj's analysis irregular.
rows.anchor: عند الجمهور تقال في كل فعل فاعلته ففعلته أفعله بصم العين ولا تكسر إلا شذوذا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh notes that the “prevail over one another” pattern does not apply to every verb; here “overcome” is the ordinary alternative.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه : كما في المفصل وليس في كل شيء يكون هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Zajjāj's analysis, the force is not to refrain from an action but to keep debating without falling short until the opponents prevail, intensifying the Prophet's resolve.
rows.anchor: لا تقصر في منازعتهم حتى يغلبوك فيها وفيه مبالغة في التثبيت

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ's report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes mansak to mean a religious law; al-Qaffāl chose this, and al-Imām calls it the closest view.
rows.anchor: وما ذكرنا من تفسير المنسك بالشريعة هو رواية عطاء عن ابن عباس واختاره القفال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Another view takes mansak as a verbal noun meaning worship or ritual; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says “they perform it” supports that reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو مصدر بمعنى النسك أي العبادة قال ابن عطية : يعطي ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other lexical proposals take mansak as a time or a place; for the place sense one might expect “performing it there,” though the expression is extended.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو اسم زمان وقيل : اسم مكان وكان الظاهر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says mansak means slaughter or sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : هو الذبح + وأخرج ذلك الحاكم وصححه

rows.speaker: الحاكم عن علي بن الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī transmit the slaughter gloss from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn; al-Ḥākim grades his report sound.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ذلك الحاكم وصححه والبيهقي عن علي بن الحسن رضي الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that mansak means slaughter.
rows.anchor: وابن أبي حاتم عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما وعبد بن حميد عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmits from ʿIkrima that mansak means slaughter.
rows.anchor: وابن أبي حاتم عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما وعبد بن حميد عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion-of-revelation account says the disputants were idolaters and the subject was sacrifice: Khuzāʿī leaders asked why believers ate what they slaughtered but not what God slaughtered.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر من أن الآية نزلت بسبب قول الخزاعيين بديل بن ورقاء وبشر بن سفيان ويزيد بن خنيس

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Shaykh al-Islām rejects limiting the dispute to sacrifices, since it would make carrion and other pagan falsehoods divinely assigned rites; the answer is that God assigned each nation its own rites, not the pagans' practices.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه شيخ الإسلام بأنه مما لا سبيل إليه أصلا كيف لا وأنه يستدعي أن يكون أكل الميتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says not to heed the pagan dispute about slaughter: sacrifice is an ancient rite prescribed for communities, not exclusive to Muhammad's community.
rows.anchor: لا تلتفت إلى نزاع المشركين في أمر الذبائح فإنا جعلنا لكل أمة من أهل الأديان ذبحاهم ذابحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For those who accept the transmitted reports, the sacrifice interpretation best explains the verse; without that commitment, the author favors the broader law-for-each-community reading already given.
rows.anchor: ومن قال بصحة الآثار وعص عليها بالنواجذ لا يكاد يجد أولى منه بيان حاصل الآية

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says the preceding rites and benefits strongly connect to “for every community We appointed a rite,” echoing the pilgrims' benefits and remembrance and showing the rite is ancient and beneficial in both worlds.
rows.anchor: أي في الشعائر منافع دينية ودنيوية كوجوب نحرها منتهية إلى البيت العتيق كالإعادة لما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī links the statement to the command to honor God's rites and says this worship is not exclusive to Muslims, since every community has its own rite.
rows.anchor: ما تقدم عطف على قوله تعالى ( ومن يعظم شعائر الله ) الخ وهو من تتمة الكلام مع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse prepares the command not to dispute, consoles and honors the Prophet, and teaches prophets to leave ignorant disputants alone while continuing to call to monotheism.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية مقدمة نهي النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم عما يوجب نزاع القوم تسلية له وتعظيم لأمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, every obstinate earlier nation had a path and religion it followed; calling its persistent practice a rite is ironic and consoles the Messenger.
rows.anchor: أو لكل أمة من الأمم الخالية المعاندة جعلنا طريقا ودينا هم ناسكوه فلا ينازعنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One coherence proposal links this to the disbelievers' continuing doubt (22:55): intervening verses console the Prophet, so he should emulate earlier prophets by ending debate after despair of their faith, with God's judgment (22:69) as support.
rows.anchor: فإن قوله تعالى ( ولا يزال الذين كفروا في مرية منه ) يوجب القلع عن إنذار القوم والإياس منهم

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf objects that the intervening passage about recompense (22:60) cannot reinforce consolation, especially on the view that it concerns fighting in the sacred month; if it could, the independent clause would still set up the prohibition that follows.
rows.anchor: تعقب في الكشف اتصاله بما ذكر بأنه لا وجه له فقد تخلل ما لا يصلح لتأكيد معنى التسلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alūsī calls the consolation linkage far-fetched and says the sūra's central theme is disputation with obstinate opponents, opened and repeatedly signaled by 22:3; that theme supports the verse's placement.
rows.anchor: والذي يدور عليه قطب هذه السورة الكريمة الكلام في مجادلة القوم ومعانديهم والنعي عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Call” addresses the disputants or all people, with the disputants included first; it means inviting them to God's oneness and worship according to the prescribed law.
rows.anchor: وادع أي وادع هؤلاء المنازعين أو الناس كافة على أنهم داخلون فيهم دخولا أوليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance is pictured as a straight path leading to truth; the path metaphor may refer either to the religion and law or to their proofs.
rows.anchor: طريق موصل إلى الحق ففيه استعارة مكنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the path metaphor, one of “straight” and “upon” may be imaginative and the other a reinforcing metaphorical extension; the sentence is an explanatory resumption giving the reason for the command.
rows.anchor: أي سوى أو أحدهما تخييل والآخر ترشيح ثم المراد بهذا الطريق إما الدين والشريعة أو أدلتها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والقرطبي والزمخشري
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Zamakhsharī take “the people” to mean the polytheists, as the following verses describe them.
rows.anchor: القرطبي والزمخشري أن المراد بالناس المشركون ويدل عليه ما ستسمعه بعد إن شاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One scholar says generic definiteness remains possible even if only some people are meant, because those people are the majority and the majority counts as the whole by custom and law.
rows.anchor: إن ما فيها من قبيل نسبة ما للبعض إلى كل فلا ينافي كون تعريفه للجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others allow “people” to denote humanity generally while its later pronouns refer to the Meccan polytheists, although they have not yet been named in the sūra.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من جوز إرادة الجنس والضمائر فيما بعد لمشركي أهل مكة وإن لم يتقدم ذكرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument that the descriptions specifically exclude monotheist sinners depends on narrow glosses of those descriptions; extending them to include such sinners is a very strained reading.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن في ذلك ارتكاب خلاف الظاهر جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is governed by “approached” and can mean either “to” or “from,” since iqtaraba takes both prepositions.
rows.anchor: واللام صلة لا قترب كما هو الظاهر وهي معنى إلى أو بمعنى من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the lām to the sense “to” is challenged as arbitrary; the author answers that both prepositions can mark an endpoint, though “to” is more characteristic of it.
rows.anchor: واقتصر بعضهم على القول بأنها بمعنى إلى فقيل فيه تحكم لحديث تعدي القرب بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that min here denotes the endpoint, citing al-Shumnī and Ibn Mālik's Arabic example equating “approached from him” with “approached him”; min is listed with this meaning, unlike ilā as an origin marker.
rows.anchor: فالحق أنها بمعنى انتهاء الغاية فانهم ذكروا أن من يجئ لذلك قال الشمني وفي الجنى الداني مثل ابن مالك

rows.speaker: اللوامح
rows.claim: Al-Lawāmiḥ says the wāw was dropped in connected recitation to avoid two sukūns, and spelling followed the pronunciation; a similar deletion appears in “yamḥu Allāhu al-bāṭil.”
rows.anchor: وفي اللوامح أنها حذفت في الدرج لالتقاء الساكنين وحملت الكتابة على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse “If the doctors were around me” illustrates a written and pronounced missing wāw whose presence is indicated by ḍamma; some grammarians call the poetic usage necessary.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء حذف الواو لفظا وكتابة والإكتفاء بالضمة الدالة عليها كما في قوله : ولو أن الأطبا كان حولي وكان مع الأطباء الأساة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One gloss defines believers as those affirming what is necessarily known to belong to the Prophet's religion, including monotheism, prophethood, bodily resurrection, and recompense.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالمؤمنين قيل إما المصدقون بما علم ضرورة أنه من دين نبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “human” first means humankind as a species, the pronoun refers to its individual descendants other than Adam; proposed antecedents involving an unstated son of Adam or omitted possessive are possible but strained.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله تعالى ( ثم جعلناه نطفة ( عائد على الجنس باعتبار أفراده المغايرة لآدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr suggests that if “human” first means Adam, the pronoun refers to his son, an unmentioned antecedent made clear by its familiarity; the author finds this unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وإذا أريد بالإنسان أولا آدم عليه السلام فالضمير على ما في البحر عائد على غير مذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses supply “offspring” after human, use Adam for his descendants, or make the pronoun refer to the extracted substance, understood as the extracted one or as water; the last means making the extract into a sperm-drop.
rows.anchor: أو على الإنسان والكلام على حذف مضاف أي ثم جعلنا نسله وقيل يراد بالإنسان أولا آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most analyses treat nuṭfa as the second object of jaʿala in the sense “make”; another analysis takes jaʿala as “create,” with nuṭfa accusative after an omitted preposition, a choice favored by some investigators.
rows.anchor: في سائر الوجوه مفعولا ثانيا للجعل على أنه بمعنى التصيير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarār originally means stable remaining, a verbal noun used intensively as a place; here it means the womb.
rows.anchor: أي مستقر وهو في الأصل مصدر من قر يقر قرارا بمعنى ثبت ثبوتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makin means securely situated; applied to the sperm-drop it is metaphorical, or it describes the womb as fixed and retaining its contents, implying that the drop is guarded and protected.
rows.anchor: أي متمكن مع أن التمكن وصف ذي المكان وهو النطفة هنا على سبيل المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlaqa is congealed blood, formed when qualities accrue to the blood and change its description; this is qualitative motion.
rows.anchor: أي دما جامدا وذلك بإضافة أعراض الدم عليها فتصيرها دما بحسب الوصف وهذا من باب الحركة في الكيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mudgha is a chew-sized piece of flesh without clear differentiation; its formation from ʿalaqa is a change in substance, like water becoming stone, as one form leaves matter and another enters.
rows.anchor: أي قطعة لحم بقدر ما يمضغ لا استبانة ولا تمايز فيها وهذا التصيير على ما قيل بحسب الذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The substantial change involves gradual shifts in readiness: matter loses its disposition for the prior form and gains one for the next until the earlier form vanishes and the new one occurs at once.
rows.anchor: ولا يزال الأول ينقص والثاني يشتد إلى أن تنتهي المادة إلى حيث تزول عنها الصورة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lump becomes bones—small and large as wisdom requires—through hardening the parts intended for bone; this is a qualitative change.
rows.anchor: وهذا أيضا تصيير بحسب الوصف فيكون من الباب الأول

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī's account implies that nuṭfa and ʿalaqa, and likewise mudgha and bone, share an underlying reality differing in qualities; ʿalaqa and mudgha differ in essence as well as qualities.
rows.anchor: وفي كلام العلامة البيضاوي إشارة ما إلى مجموع ما ذكرنا وهو يستلزم القول بأن النطفة والعلقة متحدان في الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author accepts that successive forms occur in one underlying matter throughout the stages until the human form, unless evidence establishes otherwise.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه تتعاقب في جميع هذه الأطوار على مادة واحدة صور حسب تعاقب الاستعدادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Covering the bones with flesh is like clothing them; the flesh may be leftover from the part of the lump not made bone, or fresh flesh God creates from blood in the womb.
rows.anchor: أي جعلناه ساترا لكل منها كاللباس وذلك اللحم يحتمل أن يكون من لحم المضغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bones are singled out because their shapes and hardness vary unlike the other parts; the source reports a count of 248 bones according to some.
rows.anchor: دون غيرها مما في الأطوار لأنها متغايرة هيئة وصلابة بخلاف غيرها ألا ترى عظم الساق

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم وأبان والمفضل والحسن وقتادة وهارون والجعفي ويونس عن أبي عمرو وزيد بن علي
rows.claim: They read “bone” in the singular at both occurrences, using a collective singular for few or many without ambiguity; the singular also matches the preceding stages.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم وأبان والمفضل والحسن وقتادة وهارون والجعفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular collective construction is not necessarily restricted to poetic or forced usage despite a claim attributed to Sībawayh; the cited Arabic verse says “eat within part of your belly and you will be healthy.”
rows.anchor: كما في قوله + كلوا في بعض بطنكم تعفوا + واختصاص مثل ذلك بالضرورة

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī notes that singular “bone” here creates parallelism with the singular forms used for the earlier developmental stages.
rows.anchor: وفي الإفراد هنا مشاكلة لما ذكر قبل في الأطوار كما ذكره ابن جني
